items.content_html:
My Thoughts on Prejudices and Teaching

We all have prejudices and ideas shaped by our upbringing or life experiences. It’s funny how even within the same family, personalities can be completely different just because we had different friends or grew up at different times. These biases radically change how we perceive life. As educators, we need to recognize that just like all the fingers on our hands are different, this diversity is even bigger among human beings. That’s why we are called to be inclusive and understanding.

Understanding Our Biases

  • Explicit Prejudice: When it is done consciously.

  • Implicit Prejudice: This one can exist silently in our thoughts and reactions without us even realizing it.

When we talk about education, even the smallest assumptions can deeply affect a student's school experience and their sense of belonging.

In the Classroom

It is so important to reflect on those moments in the classroom where we might misinterpret a student's participation or behavior. These readings reminded me that children express themselves in so many different ways, and as educators, we must approach learning with empathy, curiosity, and a lot of humility.

Moving Forward

The learning process is never-ending—I find myself repeating this more and more every day. This is a continuous journey. Recognizing our own biases isn't about feeling bad; it’s an act of responsibility. My goal is to keep creating spaces where students feel valued, respected, and safe to just be themselves.

A Personal Reflection

Looking back at my own experience, I realize how much graphic representation and media shape how we see other cultures. Growing up, so many stereotypes were just normalized through TV and school. (Honestly, I didn’t realize it back then, but doing this activity brought back so many memories).

At the same time, seeing public figures like Sofía Vergara openly celebrating her roots reminds me how important cultural pride and positive representation really are. However, Indigenous peoples have often been represented through incomplete or even harmful narratives, minimizing their value. This module really made me reflect on where my own assumptions come from, and the importance of continuing to listen, learn, and unlearn.

"Recognizing biases doesn’t imply guilt, but rather growth, awareness, and responsibility."

items.title: Module 2 - Connection to land
items.summary: Moving to Canada has allowed me to understand the concept of kinship from a much more personal perspective. In Colombia, I grew up…
items.content_html:
Moving to Canada has allowed me to understand the concept of kinship from a much more personal perspective. In Colombia, I grew up in a culture where family, neighbors, and the community are a huge part of your daily life. Sharing food (especially during Christmas), looking after other kids as if they were your own, having a house full of people—sometimes people we didn't even know—chatting with neighbors, or going to the corner store to buy just what you needed for the day... those things were just natural to us. Even taking the bus as the main way to get around, and especially supporting each other during hard times, are practices that are very common back home.

When I came here to start over, I realized that building a new life also means building new relationships, new support networks, and a sense of belonging. In my case, the Catholic Church has been a fundamental part of my journey during difficult moments. To be honest, the sense of community and fraternity I feel in this place is something I never even felt in my own country while practicing my religion. I’ve learned that community isn’t always about sharing the same culture or language; it’s about creating spaces where people feel heard, valued, and not alone.

This experience has deeply influenced how I see myself as an educator. Often, students walk into the classroom carrying family stories, adaptation processes, cultural differences, or emotional needs that aren't always visible. This is where the human side of our teaching needs to show up more. We have to learn to listen not just with our ears, but with all our senses—to see what’s behind every story, or what the kids who barely speak are trying to express. It's so important that children feel heard and safe, without being afraid to raise their voices. Maybe that way, the ones who feel "anonymous" can finally find a way for their ideas to reach others.

items.title: Module 2 - Power of Indigenous Kinship
items.summary: To build community and relationships in the classroom, it is vital to create an environment where students feel included, valued, and, most importantly, respected.
items.content_html:
To build community and relationships in the classroom, it is vital to create an environment where students feel included, valued, and, most importantly, respected.

I have always believed that all human beings feel more comfortable in an inclusive environment when they know they belong. This is certainly true in the classroom, and when fostered from the earliest years of life, learning becomes more meaningful because it is based not only on academics but also on emotional development,

reinforcing the importance of interpersonal relationships.

I like to create spaces in the classroom where students feel heard, not only academically but also by sharing their interests and personal experiences,activities they have done, or who they spend time with outside of school. With this approach, I aim to promote empathy, teamwork, and valuing the voices of others. Small gestures like greeting students, asking how their day was, if they slept well, or even what they had for breakfast, make them feel at home, not just in a physical space where they attend classes to learn new things.

We live in a world where relationships aren't based solely on person-to-person interaction but also include community. How we relate to our environment and how we care for the resources nature provides generates a collective responsibility. I would like to continue incorporating these ideas, as well as creating collaborative

learning opportunities where students support each other instead of competing to see who is better. Likewise, I would like to further strengthen the practice of outdoor activities based on inquiry that foster stronger connections with nature. A couple of years ago, I had the good fortune to fill in for a teacher at a school called Environmental School. What a wonderful experience! I never imagined I would enjoy it so much. Seeing the students interact with nature and their understanding of the environment was incredibly enriching. I can honestly say that my life was transformed by that experience with that educational model.

These videos and readings also reminded me that, as educators, we play a fundamental role in modeling empathy, kindness, and healthy relationships. Strengthening the bonds with students and their families helps create a classroom community where everyone feels supported and motivated to grow together.

items.title: Module 1 - Reflection
items.summary: Module 1 challenged me to rethink education beyond traditional classroom practices and academic outcomes. Through Indigenous perspectives, land-based learning, storytelling, and reflection, I…
items.content_html:
Module 1 challenged me to rethink education beyond traditional classroom practices and academic outcomes. Through Indigenous perspectives, land-based learning, storytelling, and reflection, I began to understand teaching as something deeply connected to relationships, community, identity, and the environment. The following takeaways represent the learnings that impacted me the most and that I hope to meaningfully integrate into my future teaching practice.

TAKEAWAY 1: Learning From the Land TAKEAWAY 2: First Peoples Principles of Learning TAKEAWAY 3: Meaningful Land Acknowledgements

What I learned: Working outside the classroom is deeply meaningful because it generates learning that truly lasts over time and can be naturally related to our daily lives.

Why it was important for me: It led me to question traditional education quite deeply. We shouldn't focus solely on academic content, but also on our relationship with the environment. If we value the planet and build respectful relationships with it, we will be rewarded with its abundance.

How I will apply it to my teaching practice: I will design more outdoor learning experiences, prioritize observing nature, connect scientific ideas with Indigenous knowledge, value the importance of every living being, and foster a deep sense of respect and awareness.

What I learned: Learning is inherently connected to relationships, identity, community, and reflection. When we truly internalize the meaning of this, our relationships with the environment flow naturally, without us having to force our actions.

Why it was important for me: It generated a genuine paradigm shift in my teaching approach, making it much more human, holistic, and heartfelt.

How I will apply it to my teaching practice: I believe my reflections reflect my deepest thoughts, so publishing them in my journal can serve as practical tools for other educators. Likewise, in the classroom, I will actively try to integrate students and their families to strengthen our community ties.

What I learned: Making a Land Acknowledgement cannot be just a routine or a checklist; it must be done consciously and reflectively. As educators, we teach based on our emotions, and when something isn't truly meaningful to us, we don't put the same passion into it—and students notice immediately. Therefore, we must love and respect this content first.

Why it was important for me: It helped me understand the profound relationship between territory, history, and our shared responsibility. We cannot settle for just one version of history; we must go further and respect different points of view.

How I will apply it to my teaching practice: I will investigate local territories alongside my students to co-create authentic acknowledgments. I will make sure that the depth and framing of these discussions are always appropriate to the students' developmental and chronological age.

This module helped me rethink education as something deeply connected to relationships, community, identity, and the land. It also reminded me that reconciliation is not just about learning history, but about transforming the way we teach, listen, and build respectful learning environments. I hope to continue discovering how to integrate Indigenous perspectives in meaningful and authentic ways throughout my teaching practice.

items.title: Module 1 - Introduction
items.summary: Module 1 invited me to reflect on how learning goes beyond academic achievement. Relationships, identity, respect, and emotional safety are also part of meaningful learning experiences.
items.content_html:
Module 1 invited me to reflect on how learning goes beyond academic achievement. Relationships, identity, respect, and emotional safety are also part of meaningful learning experiences.

This module also encouraged me to reflect on the importance of language, identity, and the role educators have in creating inclusive and respectful learning environments.

Sometimes students do not need perfect answers, but meaningful spaces where they feel seen and heard.
